European lobster (Homarus gammarus) females produce eggs with a substantial energetic investment, as each egg contains approximately 43.9 J  of energy. Following extrusion, the eggs are brooded on the pleopods for approximately one year, resulting in an age at birth of roughly 365 days [ab = roughly 365 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. Upon hatching, the newly emerged larvae possess a dry weight of approximately 0.0017 grams , a value derived from the caloric content of the egg and its conversion efficiency. The carapace length at settlement, when larvae transition to the benthic habitat, is about 0.6 cm , a small size that marks the beginning of the juvenile phase. The energy content of the egg has implications for the subsequent growth trajectory, as a more energetically rich egg may confer advantages in the early larval stages when resources are limited.

Juvenile development proceeds rapidly under optimal thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], laboratory studies have documented that the time since birth at metamorphosis averages just 12 days , a remarkably brief pelagic larval duration for a large decapod. By contrast, when larvae are reared at a cooler temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis extends to 35 days , illustrating the pronounced influence of temperature on developmental rate. Upon completing metamorphosis, the newly settled juveniles have a wet weight of approximately 0.154 grams . These post-metamorphic juveniles then enter a phase of rapid somatic growth, and field surveys indicate that by two years of age, individuals reared at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] attain a carapace length of 7.5 cm  and a corresponding wet weight of 300 grams . Such growth rates are among the highest recorded for European lobster, underscoring the species' capacity for rapid biomass accumulation when thermal conditions are favorable.

Sexual maturity in European lobster is achieved when individuals reach a carapace length of approximately 8.27 cm [Lp = approximately 8.27 cm], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of around 331 grams [Wwp = around 331 grams]. In the shallow coastal waters of the northeastern Atlantic, this developmental milestone is typically reached after about six years from settlement, with the time since birth at puberty being approximately 2190 days [tp = approximately 2190 days] under ambient thermal regimes averaging 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. The attainment of sexual maturity marks the beginning of reproductive activity, and mature females can produce multiple clutches during their lifespan. The maximum recorded reproductive output for this species has been estimated at 30 eggs per day [Ri = 30 eggs per day] when maintained at 8 °C [T = 8 °C], a rate that reflects both the formation and extrusion of successive clutches during the breeding season. This fecundity is a critical component of the species' life history, balancing high larval mortality with the production of numerous offspring.

The ultimate body size of Homarus gammarus is considerable, with the ultimate carapace length reaching 21.4 cm [Li = 21.4 cm], a dimension that was derived from a total length measurement of 60 centimeters using a proportional conversion based on carapace-to-total-length ratios. This large carapace length places H. gammarus among the largest decapods in the North Atlantic and is associated with high reproductive output in older females. The ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 6000 grams [Wwi = approximately 6000 grams], making it one of the largest crustaceans in European waters. Comparative studies with the American lobster (Homarus americanus) reveal that the European species attains a similar asymptotic mass, though growth increments may differ due to variation in local sea temperature and food availability. The ultimate carapace length represents the maximum size that individuals can achieve under optimal conditions, though most wild populations consist of individuals considerably smaller than this potential maximum due to environmental constraints and fishing pressure.

The lifespan of European lobster is exceptionally long for a decapod crustacean, with the maximum recorded longevity reaching at least 60 years [am = 60 years] when maintained at 8 °C [T = 8 °C], a value documented by van der Meeren and Agnalt (2000) and cited in later reviews. This extended lifespan allows individuals to reproduce over many seasons, with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to population recruitment. The species exhibits slow growth after reaching sexual maturity, with annual molting frequency decreasing substantially in older adults. Mark-recapture studies in Norwegian fjords have confirmed that some individuals may persist for more than six decades, making Homarus gammarus one of the longest-lived marine invertebrates in European coastal ecosystems. This remarkable longevity is coupled with a relatively low natural mortality rate among adults, although fishing pressure significantly truncates the age structure of exploited populations. Understanding the full lifespan potential is essential for setting sustainable harvest limits and for predicting the species' resilience to environmental change.
